lead: A 3D scene becomes a 2D picture when a camera defines the view and a projection flattens it. The camera is fixed by three things: eye position, a look-at point and an up vector. The projection is either parallel, which keeps sizes, or perspective, which divides by depth and makes far things small. Games, CAD drawings, maps, medical scans and phone AR all use this step. The same mathematics turns a list of 3D vertices into screen pixels.
prereq: You need: 2.4 for 3D transforms, 2.5 for window-to-viewport mapping and 2.6 for clipping to the view volume.

sections.h3: Camera parameters and the view matrix

blocks.text: A camera is placed in world coordinates by three parameters. The eye position E = (ex, ey, ez) is where the camera sits. The look-at point L = (lx, ly, lz) is the point it aims at. The up vector U says which way is up in the picture; it need not be the world y axis.

Build a viewing coordinate system. Forward f = normalize(L − E) points from the eye to the target. U must not be parallel to f; if it is, pick another up vector. Right r = normalize(f × U), and up u = normalize(r × f). These are unit vectors. A world point P becomes a viewing point by subtracting E and taking dot products: x_v = r·(P − E), y_v = u·(P − E), z_v = f·(P − E).
M_view = [ r_x r_y r_z −r·E ; u_x u_y u_z −u·E ; f_x f_y f_z −f·E ; 0 0 0 1 ]
blocks.where: E is the eye position, f = normalize(L − E) is forward, r = normalize(f × U) is right and u = normalize(r × f) is up; r·E means the dot product. This matrix is an orthonormal change of basis plus a translation. The 3×3 block has determinant −1, so it includes a mirror and is not a pure rotation.

blocks.text: After this matrix the camera sits at the origin and looks along +z. The matrix has no scale and no perspective; it only changes coordinates. A pinhole camera adds a projection plane at z = d in front of the eye. Camera models with focal length and principal point, plus this pose, are fitted to image points in pose estimation and phone AR.

Parallel projection sends every point along the same direction onto the projection plane. Orthographic projection is the case where that direction is perpendicular to the plane. Oblique projection uses a slanted direction, so it shows a front face plus a receding side. Neither divides by depth: a 10 cm cube at 1 m and at 100 m draws the same size.
Perspective projection models a pinhole camera. Put the centre of projection at the origin and the projection plane at z = d, with d > 0. A point P = (x, y, z), z > 0, projects to:

blocks.where: P = (x, y, z) is the 3D point in camera coordinates measured in metres, d is the distance from the eye to the projection plane in metres, and x′, y′ are coordinates on that plane in metres. The ratio d/z is the scale.

blocks.text: A point twice as far away has half the scale, so distant objects look smaller. The angle the plane subtends at the eye sets the field of view. At z = 0 the divide has no finite result. For z < 0 the formula returns a finite but meaningless point on the plane, because the point lies behind the eye. Geometry with z ≤ 0 must be clipped at the near plane before the divide.

sections.h3: Vanishing points and the view volume

blocks.text: Under perspective, parallel 3D lines that are not parallel to the picture plane appear to meet at a vanishing point. The point is the projection of the direction of the lines. One-point perspective has one principal axis that is not parallel to the picture plane (it is perpendicular to it), two-point has two, and three-point has all three. Tall buildings viewed from below often use three-point perspective.

The set of points that can appear is the view volume. For parallel projection it is a box with left, right, bottom, top, near and far planes. For perspective it is a frustum, a truncated pyramid with its apex at the eye. Geometry outside this volume is clipped. Clipping happens in the view volume before the perspective divide, so no coordinate becomes infinite as z approaches 0.

After clipping, the divide maps the frustum to a cube in normalised device coordinates. The window-to-viewport map in 2.5 places that cube on the screen. The line and polygon clipping algorithms in 2.6 and 2.7 work on the edges of the volume. A box view volume needs no divide; a frustum always does.

figure.caption: The tree splits projections by whether a depth divide is used. Parallel keeps object size; perspective divides by depth and can show one, two or three vanishing points.

spec.aria: A two-level tree splitting projections into parallel, with orthographic and oblique children, and perspective, with one-, two- and three-point children.

examples.question: A perspective camera has its centre of projection at the origin and its projection plane at z = 3. Project the point P(2, 4, 6) and the point Q(2, 4, 12) onto the plane. Give both screen points and explain the change in size.
steps: The projection plane is z = d = 3, and the centre of projection is the origin, so use x′ = x·d/z and y′ = y·d/z.
Q is twice as far from the eye as P. Its image coordinates are half of P's, so the image size falls as 1/z.
examples.answer: P′ = (1, 2) and Q′ = (0.5, 1) in the projection plane's length unit; the farther point Q lands at half the distance from the centre of the picture.
examples.check:
d = 3
for x, y, z in [(2, 4, 6), (2, 4, 12)]:
    print(f"{x * d / z:g}")
    print(f"{y * d / z:g}")

traps: Using z = d in the divide instead of the point's actual depth z. The plane distance d is fixed; z changes with each point.
Applying a perspective divide in a parallel projection. Orthographic and oblique projections have no divide by depth.
Forgetting that the divide uses the depth along the camera's view axis. After an arbitrary view matrix, world z is not the same as camera depth.
Projecting points with z ≤ 0. At z = 0 the divide has no finite result; for z < 0 the formula gives a meaningless finite point behind the eye. Clip at the near plane first.
Calling the perspective view volume a box. It is a frustum; the box is the parallel projection view volume.

quiz.q: Name the two main classes of projection and one subtype of each.
quiz.a: Parallel: orthographic or oblique. Perspective: one-point, two-point or three-point.

quiz.q: Why does a parallel projection have no vanishing point?
quiz.a: All projection rays are parallel, so parallel 3D lines stay parallel in the image and never meet.

quiz.q: A perspective camera has the centre of projection at the origin and the projection plane at z = 4. Project P(3, 6, 9).
An orthographic projection drops the z coordinate onto the plane z = 0. Where does the point (2, 4, 6) land?
quiz.a: The x and y coordinates do not change, so the point lands at (2, 4) on z = 0.

quiz.q: Why is clipping done before the perspective divide, not after it?
quiz.a: As z approaches 0, x·d/z and y·d/z grow without bound or change sign. Clipping against the near plane in the view volume removes such geometry first, so the divide never produces infinite or meaningless coordinates.

quiz.q: A cube is drawn in two-point perspective. How many vanishing points are visible and why?
quiz.a: Two principal axes of the cube are oblique to the picture plane, so each set of parallel edges gives a vanishing point. The third principal axis is parallel to the picture plane, so its edges do not converge.

quiz.q: What shape is the perspective view volume, and what shape is the parallel view volume?
quiz.a: The perspective view volume is a frustum, a truncated pyramid with its apex at the eye. The parallel view volume is a box.

beyond: Not for the exam. Camera calibration estimates focal length, principal point and lens distortion from images of a known pattern. Visual SLAM and AR frameworks chain camera pose with projection to track a phone in a room. Structure from motion recovers 3D points and camera positions from many photos. Search for camera intrinsics, extrinsics, pinhole model and perspective-n-point.
